Issue #1453: Local named functions can allocate dead closures after inlining

<!--
Proposed title: Local named functions can allocate dead closures after inlining
Suggested labels: bug, performance, high reward

This file is ready to pass to `gh issue create --body-file`. The comment is
intentionally hidden when rendered on GitHub.
-->

## Summary

A small nonrecursive local function written with `fun` can allocate a fresh
closure on every execution even though its only call is eventually inlined. The
semantically equivalent `val f = fn ...` spelling is inlined earlier and does
not allocate.

In the example below, the late BVL inliner removes the call to `bump` but leaves
a dead 24-byte closure allocation inside the loop. Over 100 million iterations,
that is 2.4 GB (about 2.24 GiB) of avoidable allocation. The named form was
1.76× slower in paired x64-64 measurements.

## Reproducer

Named local function:

```sml
fun loop n acc =
  if n = 0 then acc
  else
    let fun bump x = x + 1
    in loop (n - 1) (acc + bump n) end;

fun main () =
  let val n = Option.valOf (Int.fromString (List.hd (CommandLine.arguments ())))
  in print_int (loop n 0); print "\n" end;

main ();
```

The control changes only the local binding:

```diff
-    let fun bump x = x + 1
+    let val bump = fn x => x + 1
     in loop (n - 1) (acc + bump n) end;
```

From an x64-64 build directory containing `cake` and `basis_ffi.c`, save the
variants as `/tmp/named.cml` and `/tmp/anonymous.cml`, then run:

```sh
./cake < /tmp/named.cml > /tmp/named.S
./cake < /tmp/anonymous.cml > /tmp/anonymous.S
cc -O2 /tmp/named.S basis_ffi.c -lm -o /tmp/named
cc -O2 /tmp/anonymous.S basis_ffi.c -lm -o /tmp/anonymous

env CML_HEAP_SIZE=32 CML_STACK_SIZE=16 taskset -c 2 \
  /tmp/named 100000000 > /tmp/named.out
env CML_HEAP_SIZE=32 CML_STACK_SIZE=16 taskset -c 2 \
  /tmp/anonymous 100000000 > /tmp/anonymous.out
cmp /tmp/named.out /tmp/anonymous.out

/usr/bin/time -f 'named: %e s' \
  env CML_HEAP_SIZE=32 CML_STACK_SIZE=16 taskset -c 2 \
  /tmp/named 100000000 > /dev/null
/usr/bin/time -f 'anonymous: %e s' \
  env CML_HEAP_SIZE=32 CML_STACK_SIZE=16 taskset -c 2 \
  /tmp/anonymous 100000000 > /dev/null
```

Both variants print `5000000150000000`.

## Measurements

| Form | Median | Interquartile range | Relative |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| local `fun bump` | 0.640 s | 0.620–0.670 s | 1.76× |
| local `val bump = fn` | 0.365 s | 0.350–0.385 s | 1.00× |

## Generated-code evidence

After `clos_known`, the named form still contains a `Letrec` and an annotated
application of `bump`. The anonymous form has already substituted the body at
the call site.

After `bvl_inline`, the named loop has this shape:

```text
(let
  (c <- (Cons closure_tag 0 (Label loop_bump_clos)))
  (call loop
    (Add (let (d <- n) (Add 1 d)) acc)
    (Sub 1 n)))
```

The `Add 1 d` is the inlined body of `bump`, while `c` is never read. The closure
allocation is therefore dead, but it survives through final code generation.
The x64 loop checks for 24 bytes of heap and stores the closure header, code
pointer, and empty environment on every iteration. The anonymous loop has no
corresponding heap check or allocation.

The named executable also retains separate `loop_bump` worker and closure-wrapper
symbols; the anonymous executable does not retain a `bump` symbol.

## Cause

`clos_known` treats anonymous `Fn` and `Letrec` differently:

- an anonymous `Fn` can receive a body-carrying `Clos` approximation
  ([`clos_knownScript.sml`](https://github.com/CakeML/cakeml/blob/0fe74ee25d03a7d6d72892927edcaf5ae9677e10/compiler/backend/clos_knownScript.sml#L610-L616));
- every `Letrec`, including this single function with no recursive occurrence,
  receives `ClosNoInline`
  ([`clos_knownScript.sml`](https://github.com/CakeML/cakeml/blob/0fe74ee25d03a7d6d72892927edcaf5ae9677e10/compiler/backend/clos_knownScript.sml#L617-L629)).

`decide_inline` can body-inline only `Clos`; `ClosNoInline` merely enables a
direct-call annotation
([`clos_knownScript.sml`](https://github.com/CakeML/cakeml/blob/0fe74ee25d03a7d6d72892927edcaf5ae9677e10/compiler/backend/clos_knownScript.sml#L511-L529)).
Closure conversion consequently materializes the local closure before the BVL
pass gets an opportunity to inline its call; the single-function `Letrec`
lowering constructs a closure block
([`clos_to_bvlScript.sml`](https://github.com/CakeML/cakeml/blob/0fe74ee25d03a7d6d72892927edcaf5ae9677e10/compiler/backend/clos_to_bvlScript.sml#L453-L466)).
The later inliner substitutes the worker body but does not perform the
higher-level use/escape cleanup needed to remove the already-materialized
closure, wrapper, and worker.

This is a source-spelling performance cliff, not a correctness problem.

## Expected behavior

For a small local function that is provably nonrecursive and nonescaping,
equivalent `fun f x = e` and `val f = fn x => e` forms should produce equivalent
optimized code. If all uses have been inlined or converted to direct worker
calls, no closure should be allocated.

## Possible implementation direction

1. Analyze dependencies within `Letrec` groups and identify singleton or
   otherwise nonrecursive SCCs.
2. Give small nonrecursive members body-carrying approximations, subject to the
   existing inlining and growth limits, instead of assigning every member
   `ClosNoInline`.
3. Split recursive groups into dependency SCCs where possible; retain the
   conservative treatment for genuinely recursive members.
4. Add post-inlining closure use/escape cleanup so a closure allocation and its
   wrapper/worker can be removed when no value use remains.

The first two steps should fix this minimal case by allowing the inlining to
happen before closure conversion.

## Regression coverage

- Compare equivalent nonrecursive local `fun` and `val ... = fn ...` forms.
- Check optimized IR or emitted code to ensure the hot loop contains no closure
  construction or heap-space check.
- Check that an unused wrapper and worker are removed in sealed compilation.
- Cover self recursion and mutually recurs

A maintainer on the project CategoricalData/hydra (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #697: CL/EL flat loaders should load by dependency order, not alphabetical (durable fix for the load-order class)

## Problem

The Common Lisp and Emacs Lisp "flat" module loaders
(`overlay/common-lisp/hydra-kernel/.../loader.lisp`, `overlay/emacs-lisp/.../loader.el`) load generated
`hydra.*` modules in **alphabetical order** — `(append priority (sort remaining #'string<))` — and ignore
`manifest.json`'s dependency information. When a generated module references another that sorts *after* it
alphabetically, the consumer loads before its dependency exists → unbound-symbol crash at load time.

This bit us in the #416 marquee: `hydra.build.langexpansion` / `hydra.build.syncmatrix` reference
`hydra.build.registry`, but `registry` sorts after them → the loaders crashed both dialects (fixed as
`26e052fd15` by pinning `build/registry` into the loaders' `priority` list). Scheme (R7RS `import`) and
Clojure (`:require`) resolve dependencies natively and are immune; only the two flat loaders have this gap.

## Why the current fix is a patch, not a cure

`26e052fd15` (and the earlier CL/EL priority-list entries) hand-pin specific leaf modules into a `priority`
list ahead of the alphabetical remainder. That works for *today's* known cross-references, but **every future
`hydra.*` module whose name sorts before a module it depends on re-triggers the crash** and needs another
manual priority-list entry. It scales as whack-a-mole with the module count. The per-file 10-retry the loaders
already do does **not** cover cross-*file* forward references, which is why load order matters.

## Durable fix

Make the CL/EL flat loaders load in **dependency order** derived from `manifest.json`'s per-module dependency
lists (topological sort), instead of alphabetical + hand-maintained priority. This kills the whole class: any
DAG-valid module set loads correctly with no per-module tuning.

## Scope

Two files (`loader.lisp`, `loader.el`). Read the already-emitted `manifest.json`, topo-sort by declared deps,
load in that order; drop the alphabetical sort + the now-unnecessary hand-pinned priority entries.
Behavior-equivalent for today's graph; robust for all future ones.

Relates to the CL/EL loader fix `26e052fd15`. Follow-up to #416.

Issue #109574: Lazy DNS resolution for remote_servers hosts at startup

### Company or project name

AWS

### Use case

When ClickHouse starts, it builds the cluster topology in setClustersConfig before the server is fully started. Constructing each `Cluster::Address` calls isLocal, which does a synchronous, blocking getaddrinfo for every host in remote_servers (`Cluster::Address::Address` → `isLocal` → `getResolvedAddress` → `DNSResolver::resolveAddress`, `Cluster.cpp:136`).

This resolution is already non-fatal (`getResolvedAddress` catches all exceptions and returns {}, `Cluster.cpp:80-92`, so [#106648](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106648) is correctly closed). The remaining problem is that it is synchronous and eager: startup walks the entire remote_servers list, resolving each host, before it finishes coming up. When DNS is slow or unavailable in a large cluster, startup is held up for the whole list.

This scales badly. With a cluster of 500+ servers and the default `resolv.conf (timeout:5, attempts:2)`, each unresolvable host blocks for the full resolver timeout before it gives up, and the lookups run serially. During a DNS outage that adds up to a startup time on the order of 3 to 4 hours, which is far beyond any liveness or startup probe budget, so the k8s nodes are killed and restarted before they can come up and loops for the duration of the outage.

The result of DNS resolution being computed is not critical to startup. `is_local` only decides whether a distributed query to a co-located shard takes the local shortcut (prefer_localhost_replica). If it is unset, the query uses the normal remote path, and the background `DNSCacheUpdater` corrects `is_local` once DNS resolves. 

For static stability, a node should be able to start and become fully ready without depending on the DNS or availability of its peers. A node's own health should not be a function of whether other nodes are currently resolvable.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Lazy resolution: resolve cluster host addresses on first use rather than eagerly at config-load time. Build the cluster topology without calling `DNS`, and let the connection pool resolve each host when a query first needs it (it already resolves lazily on use). `is_local` for a co-located shard is then determined later, or refreshed by the background `DNSCacheUpdater`, rather than gating startup.

This removes DNS from the startup path entirely, so a node reaches full readiness regardless of peer DNS state. The only effect during a DNS outage is that a distributed query to a co-located shard takes the remote path until resolution succeeds, which is already how transient DNS failures are handled after startup.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

  - Tune `resolv.conf` (options timeout:1 attempts:1). Cuts each failed lookup from the default timeout to about a second, so a full-outage startup drops from hours to minutes. Works today with no code change, but it only shortens the window rather than removing the dependency, it applies to every lookup on the host (not just startup), and startup readiness is still coupled to peer `DNS`. A useful mitigation, not a fix.
  - Use IP addresses instead of hostnames in `remote_servers`. `resolveIPAddressImpl` short-circuits on IP literals, so no `getaddrinfo` happens. This defeats the purpose of DNS-based service discovery and is impractical with dynamic pod addressing in Kubernetes.
  - Bind the listening sockets (or just `/ping`) before resolving `remote_servers`. Makes the liveness probe pass early, but the server still is not ready: metadata and cluster setup remain  blocked. A pod that answers `/ping` while unable to serve is arguably worse, so this addresses liveness without addressing readiness.
  - Bounded / parallel eager resolution (short per-host timeout, resolve concurrently, mark slow hosts non-local for now). Shortens the startup stall, but still couples startup to DNS being reachable, so a long enough outage still degrades startup. Lazy resolution removes the dependency entirely and is preferred.
  - Existing DNS settings (`disable_internal_dns_cache`, `dns_max_consecutive_failures`, `dns_cache_update_period`). These govern the runtime cache and its background refresher, not the synchronous startup pass. The cache is empty at cold start, so none of them help the first config load.

### Additional context

- Related: [106648](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106648) (closed; asked for non-fatal startup resolution, which already exists. This issue is about resolution being eager and synchronous at startup, not about it being fatal.)

Issue #113734: JSON parsing: make `JSONExtractTree` object traversal allocation-free per key (reusable path buffer + two-bit duplicate-key masks) — JSONAsObject workloads parse 25–34% faster, peak memory down (pre-existing cost, not a regression)

### Company or project name

_No response_

### Describe the situation

**This is not a regression report.** The cost described here is pre-existing — the investigation's frozen objective records it as present in both 26.6 and 26.7 — and this issue proposes a general allocation-avoidance improvement to the JSON parsing hot path: a free win, with a validated candidate patch attached.

The JSON object-traversal loop in `src/Formats/JSONExtractTree.cpp` (`ObjectJSONNode::traverseAndInsert`) does two kinds of per-key allocation work on **every key of every traversed object**:

1. **A `String` per key per object from `buildChildPath`.** The traversal builds each child's full dotted path as a fresh `String` returned by value (v26.7.1.1315-stable `src/Formats/JSONExtractTree.cpp:2013` on the hot path; `buildChildPath` definition at `:2122-2132`). A single reusable buffer — children append their key in place and truncate back on the way out — removes the per-key construction entirely.
2. **Node-based duplicate-key bookkeeping.** Two per-object `std::unordered_map<std::string_view, std::unordered_set<JSONElementType>>` structures (`key_element_types` at `:1957`, `visited_keys` at `:2010`) spend a map node, a set bucket array and a set node on every key, whether or not anything is duplicated. `JSONElementType` is a two-value enum (`:2428-2432`), so the set of types seen for one key fits losslessly in a two-bit mask; an open-addressing `HashMap<std::string_view, UInt8>` (the idiom already used for per-row key maps in `src/Processors/Formats/Impl`) makes the bookkeeping allocation-free per key.

Issue #15517: [Performance] ModelPatcher creates a new namedtuple class for every weight backup

### Custom Node Testing

- [x] I have tried disabling custom nodes and the issue persists (see [how to disable custom nodes](https://docs.comfy.org/troubleshooting/custom-node-issues#step-1%3A-test-with-all-custom-nodes-disabled) if you need help)

## Expected Behavior

`ModelPatcher.backup` entries should reuse one tuple type. For `N` backed-up weights:

```python
len(self.backup) == N
len({type(entry) for entry in self.backup.values()}) == 1
```

Creating and clearing backup entries should not generate a new class and its associated cyclic objects for every weight.

## Actual Behavior

`comfy/model_patcher.py` calls `collections.namedtuple()` inside two per-key hot paths. Because `collections.namedtuple()` creates a new class on every call, ComfyUI creates one distinct `Dimension` type per backed-up weight:

```python
self.backup[key] = collections.namedtuple(
    "Dimension", ["weight", "inplace_update"]
)(weight.to(device=self.offload_device, copy=inplace_update), inplace_update)
```

and:

```python
self.backup[key] = collections.namedtuple(
    "Dimension", ["weight", "inplace_update"]
)(weight, False)
```

Therefore:

```python
len({type(entry) for entry in self.backup.values()}) == len(self.backup)
```

Each generated class brings its own methods, closure cells, descriptors, `staticmethod`, `classmethod`, and two `_tuplegetter` objects. Repeated model patch/load/unload cycles generate large amounts of class-shaped cyclic garbage.

In one 178.1-second production observation window, the GC-tracked heap grew with the exact signature of approximately 925 newly generated two-field namedtuple classes:

```text
total tracked    +65,105
type                 +931
staticmethod         +925
classmethod          +925
_tuplegetter        +1,850
function            +5,568
cell                +8,365
tuple              +23,049
frozenset          +17,550

Gen 2 collections:          +13
Objects collected by Gen 2: +310,277
Average per Gen 2:          ~23,867
```

In an isolated reproduction using the actual upstream assignment, 2,000 backup entries created 2,000 distinct classes. Clearing the backup made Gen 2 collect approximately 58,000–62,000 class-related cyclic objects, depending on the Python version. The shared-type implementation created one class and no per-entry class-related cyclic garbage.

This reproduces the core allocation behavior on a clean ComfyUI checkout without loading custom nodes or requiring a workflow/model file:

2. Save the following as `/tmp/reproduce_model_patcher_namedtuple_gc.py`:

   model = torch.nn.Module()
   keys = []

       key = f"weight_{index}"
       keys.append(key)
       model.register_parameter(
           key,
           torch.nn.Parameter(torch.ones(1)),

   patcher = ModelPatcher(
       model,
       load_device=torch.device("cpu"),

Issue #2251: Project version control: commit and recall versions inside the project

## Vision

A project accumulates versions internally instead of spawning copies of itself on disk. The project is the parent object: the user commits versions of the working state and recalls them from inside the app. This kills the `MySong_final_v3` folder plague, and copies of a project can never share the sample pool anyway, while versions inside the project always do.

## Model

Object store + manifests, with the working tip as just an unfrozen version (git's architecture, minus branches):

- **Zero cost until first commit.** An unversioned project stays a plain `.mgd` document, exactly as today.
- **On first commit the project migrates to an object store.** The document splits at its natural seams (project info, per-track record, per-track clips, per-track automation); each slice is stored once as a compressed blob in `versions/objects/`, content-addressed by hash. The `.mgd` becomes a small manifest: the slice hashes that make up the working tip. The load path resolves either form in one centralized spot in the serializer.
- **Saves get safer, not just smaller.** Instead of rewriting one big JSON (a crash mid-write can lose the project), a save appends immutable blobs for the changed slices, then atomically swaps the tiny manifest.
- **Commit is near-free.** The blobs already exist from saving; committing freezes the current manifest with message, timestamp, and provenance.
- **Dedup is automatic.** Slices untouched between versions are shared, so a version costs roughly what actually changed. No diff chains and no patch replay: every version is independently restorable from its manifest, and a damaged blob affects only the versions that reference it, never the rest of history.
- **Media stays external and shared** in the project's media folder, so versions add JSON-sized blobs, not duplicated projects. Media garbage collection (if any) must treat files referenced by any version as live.
- **Blob GC.** Saves orphan the blobs the tip no longer references; on save or close, drop blobs referenced by neither the tip nor any version. Safe: single-writer local store.
- **Commits pin data.** Deleting a track or clip from the live session never loses anything a committed version holds.
- **History is one flat timeline.** One snapshot type; restore rebuilds the document from a manifest.

## Restore semantics (no branches)

The working session is always the tip. Restoring never checks out into the past: it copies the chosen snapshot forward into the working session, and the next commit appends to the same timeline (with provenance, e.g. "from v2"). Branches are structurally impossible. These are Google Docs / Time Machine semantics rather than git's DAG, which exists to merge parallel collaborators that a project here doesn't have.

Before a restore, auto-commit the current working state so nothing unsaved is lost.

## Partial recall

Recall can also pull a single aspect out of a snapshot instead of the whole thing. First case: **mix-only recall**, overlaying the snapshot's per-track device chains, faders, pans and sends onto the current arrangement by trackId. The overlay never creates or deletes tracks; entries for tracks that no longer exist stay inert in the snapshot. A "mix" tag on a commit is plain metadata for filtering the version list, not a different commit type.

## Out of scope

- Branching, merging, diff views.
- Cross-project version sharing.

## Problem

The central `coverage-evidence` sandbox (`OpenCode Review Dispatch` workflow, `coverage-evidence` job, "Measure test and docstring evidence" step) blocks OpenCode approval for LineageWeave PRs with a spurious FAIL that has nothing to do with the PR's actual code.

## Evidence

Run [32628753453](https://github.com/ContextualWisdomLab/.github/actions/runs/32628753453) against `ContextualWisdomLab/LineageWeave#417` at head `91b7e1cd914442e61e322620f194d1ba9da48567` (a clean, unrelated docs/backend PR — TEPP topic-lineage ADR + analysis-run scaffolding). Result: `Coverage Decision: FAIL`, `Failure count: 4`. All 4 are environment/tooling failures in the sandbox itself, not the PR:

**1. Python test collection: 39/39 test files fail to import**
```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'asyncpg'
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'psycopg2'
```
Every test file that imports LineageWeave's backend app modules fails collection (`1 skipped, 39 errors in 1.57s`). `asyncpg>=0.29.0` and `psycopg2-binary>=2.9.12` are genuine, declared dependencies in LineageWeave's `pyproject.toml` — they're not missing from the PR, they're missing from the sandbox's `pip install --require-hashes -r /tmp/requirements-opencode-review-ci-hashes.txt` step. That hash-pinned requirements file appears stale or generated from an incomplete source relative to LineageWeave's actual `pyproject.toml`.

**2. JS/TS dependency install: unsupported pnpm flag**
```
$ corepack pnpm install --offline --frozen-lockfile --trust-lockfile --ignore-scripts --store-dir ...
ERROR  Unknown option: 'trust-lockfile'
Did you mean 'frozen-lockfile'? Use "--config.unknown=value" to force an unknown option.
```
`--trust-lockfile` isn't a valid pnpm flag on the version installed in the sandbox (pnpm 11.17.0 per LineageWeave's own CI). This looks like either a typo for `--frozen-lockfile` (already present separately in the same command) or a flag from a different pnpm major version.

**3 & 4. Cascading failures from #2**
JS/TS test coverage (`vitest: not found` — `node_modules` never got installed because of #2) and JS/TS coverage threshold (`no coverage summary files were produced`) both fail as a direct downstream consequence.

This is a hard block, not a slow-down: `coverage-evidence` failing means OpenCode explicitly posts `REQUEST_CHANGES` ("OpenCode cannot approve yet because required coverage evidence did not pass") regardless of the PR's actual content. Since `asyncpg`/`psycopg2` are core LineageWeave backend dependencies, this should reproduce on essentially any LineageWeave PR that touches backend/tests — i.e., this is very likely blocking a large fraction of the current org-wide review backlog independently of `.github#624`'s model-pool issue.

## Not attempting a fix

The install pipeline here is deliberately hardened (hash-pinned `pip install --require-hashes --only-binary=:all:`, VCS-locked base dependencies with import-root/symlink/compiled-extension validation, trusted-source materialization without a repository token) — consistent with the same kind of anti-tampering design already documented as under active maintenance elsewhere in this org's CI. I don't have visibility into how `requirements-opencode-review-ci-hashes.txt` or the pnpm invocation are generated/maintained, so I'm not guessing at a fix here; recording the evidence for whoever owns that generation step.

Issue #810: security: make central dependency-review unavailability fail closed

## Organization-wide security-gate defect

The central required workflow `.github/workflows/security-scan.yml` currently documents dependency review as a **HARD diff-scoped gate**, but deliberately converts GitHub dependency-review API `403`/`404` responses into a successful skip:

```text
Dependency review is unavailable for ${REPOSITORY}; skipping dependency-review hard gate.
```

The job then exits `0`, skips `actions/dependency-review-action`, and allows the bundled required **Security Scan** to conclude success.

This is not equivalent to a clean dependency review and creates a false-green supply-chain result.

## Exact downstream evidence

`ContextualWisdomLab/EgressWeave` is public. On EgressWeave PR #66 exact head `c038a9509d1a8eae8561cc9081e67e12bd373d42`, Security Scan run `31108241013`, dependency-review job `92638903658`, the exact comparison

`10d0c51daf2ad278d66f43be479df8cf6b08ba6d...c038a9509d1a8eae8561cc9081e67e12bd373d42`

returned HTTP `403`. The workflow emitted the skip warning, did not execute `actions/dependency-review-action`, and still concluded success. EgressWeave tracks the buyer-visible downstream blocker in ContextualWisdomLab/EgressWeave#76.

GitHub's current documentation states that dependency review and the dependency-review action are available for all public GitHub.com repositories when dependency graph is enabled. The dependency-review REST API may be used without authentication for public resources; with a fine-grained token, `Contents: read` is sufficient. Therefore a `403` on a public non-fork repository is not valid clean-review evidence and requires diagnosis rather than normalization to success.

## Current integration opportunity

Open PR #799 already changes this same central workflow and exact-head dependency-review checkout contracts from protected `main` `f070c504c1cb06891b800d7ab0cf6ac7d3cf8eae`. If #799's exact head remains suitable, prefer extending that PR test-first rather than opening a competing workflow PR. If #799 advances incompatibly, keep this as a separate bounded follow-up from then-current protected main.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Add an immutable RED contract proving the current `403`/`404` success-skip path is forbidden.
- [ ] Preserve explicit exact head repository + exact head SHA checkout and exact `BASE_SHA...HEAD_SHA` comparison binding.
- [ ] A `200` support probe may proceed to the immutable-pinned `actions/dependency-review-action` hard gate.
- [ ] A `403`, `404`, malformed/empty HTTP status, transport failure, timeout, truncated response, unexpected status, or other inability to establish dependency-review support must **not** be reported as dependency-review `passed`.
- [ ] For public repositories, fail closed on dependency-review unavailability and emit an actionable error telling operators to verify repository dependency-graph/security configuration and GitHub service behavior.
- [ ] Do not guess a root cause from `403`; record repository visibility, exact base/head, and status without leaking credentials or response bodies that may contain sensitive detail.
- [ ] If support for private/internal repositories lacking GitHub Code Security is required, implement only an explicit organization-governed exception with documented compensating controls and an unmistakable `not-applicable` result. Do not infer N/A from `403`/`404` inside branch-controlled code.
- [ ] Preserve least privilege: `contents: read`, no repository/ref/package/release write, no OIDC, no model credential, no caller-controlled code under a privileged identity.
- [ ] Preserve immutable action pins and the independent OSV, Trivy, Scorecard, CodeQL/SAST/secret surfaces; do not make another scanner a semantic substitute for dependency review.
- [ ] Add/update beginner-readable doctoring with APA 7 primary GitHub references and one `[Unreleased]` Security entry; no release/version bump.
- [ ] Prove focused contracts and the complete central test/coverage/docstring/compile quality contract, then obtain exact-current-head Security Scan and all other required central checks/reviews plus qualifying independent non-author approval before merge.

## Trust boundary

This is a required-workflow control-plane fix. Do not add a branch-local publisher, `contents: write`, push/rebase/merge authority, workflow self-modification, `-X ours/theirs`, temporary write-capable repair workflow, or execution of model-modified source under a write credential. Any repair branch must remain exact-head bound and stale-head refusing.

Implement the first production-grade Automated Essay Evaluation vertical module for `fast-mlsirm`, grounded in the *Routledge International Handbook of Automated Essay Evaluation* and recent psychometric research on LLM-based essay scoring.

fast_mlsirm.scoring                   # shared assessment, policy, observation, evidence, result, and engine contracts from #473/#489

- scorer family and version

- examinee/essay proficiency
- task or prompt difficulty
- rubric-dimension difficulty
- human/AI rater severity

- exact and adjacent agreement
- Pearson/Spearman association as descriptive statistics only

- range-compression detection
- subgroup standardized mean differences

Issue #508: Diamond task dependencies falsely rejected as circular in run, lanes run and lanes validate

## Summary

A **diamond dependency** — two tasks sharing a common dependency — is reported as a circular dependency and hard-fails. This is an ordinary config shape (e.g. `test` and `lint` both depending on `build`), and it breaks three commands: `fledge run`, `fledge lanes run`, and `fledge lanes validate`.

## Reproduction

```toml

d = "echo d"

[tasks.b]
cmd = "echo b"
deps = ["d"]

[tasks.c]
cmd = "echo c"
deps = ["d"]

[tasks.a]
cmd = "echo a"
deps = ["b", "c"]

[lanes.build]
description = "diamond deps, no cycle"
steps = [{ task = "a" }]
```

Graph: `a → [b, c]`, `b → [d]`, `c → [d]`. A DAG. `d` has no dependencies at all.

```

d

b

$ fledge lanes run build
  ▶️ Running task: d
  ▶️ Running task: b
error: Lane 'build' failed at step 1 (a) after 1ms: Circular dependency detected: task 'd' depends on itself (chain: c → a → d → b)

$ fledge lanes validate
  error: Circular dependency detected involving task 'a'
error: Validation failed
```

`fledge lanes run build --dry-run` **passes** — it uses the one correct implementation (see below), so dry-run and real run disagree.

Note `d` is a bare string task with no `deps` key, so "task 'd' depends on itself" is impossible on its face. The `chain:` in the second message is a `HashSet` iterated in arbitrary order, not a path — `c → a → d → b` is not a walk in this graph.

## Root cause

There are **four** cycle detectors. One is correct; three share the same defect.

| Location | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `src/lanes/mod.rs:506` `check_dep_cycle` | **Correct** — `visiting.remove(name)` after recursing (proper backtracking) |
| `src/run.rs:282` `execute_task` | Buggy — `visited` accumulates, never removed |
| `src/lanes/execute.rs:384` `execute_task_recursive` | Buggy — same |
| `src/lanes/validate.rs:122` `validate_lanes` | Buggy — same, iterative variant |

The three buggy ones conflate two distinct sets:

- **"currently on the recursion stack"** — revisiting this *is* a cycle.
- **"already completed"** — revisiting this is just a shared dependency, and should be skipped, not rejected.

`check_dep_cycle` gets this right by removing the node on the way out. The others keep one accumulating `visited` set, so the second path into any shared node is misread as a cycle. In `run.rs` the same set is also doing double duty as run-once dedup, which is why the bug and the dedup logic are tangled there.

## Suggested fix

Two sets, or one set plus backtracking:

- Cycle detection: an on-stack set, inserted before recursing and removed after — i.e. what `check_dep_cycle` already does.
- Run-once dedup: a separate `completed` set that is only ever added to; a hit means "skip, already ran", not "error".

Given `check_dep_cycle` is already correct and already used by the dry-run path, the cleanest fix is to delete the three duplicates and have all callers use it, keeping a separate `completed` set in the two executors for dedup.

## Test coverage gap

`validate_lanes` has no unit tests — the existing `validate_circular_deps` test exercises `check_dep_cycle`, the one implementation that isn't broken. A regression test should assert that a diamond **passes** in all four paths, and that a genuine cycle (`a → b → a`) still fails in all four.

## Impact

Any project whose task graph has a shared dependency cannot run it. Since sharing a `build`/`setup` task between `test` and `lint` is a normal pattern, and `--dry-run` disagrees with the real run, this is likely to be hit and confusing when it is.

Issue #11: Implement Commit concrete class (history as a Merkle DAG)

## Intended outcome

Add the third concrete object type: `Commit`. A `Commit` is the object that records **"this tree is now the state of the repository"** — it points to a `Tree` (the snapshot), optionally to parent `Commit`(s) (the history), plus author metadata and a message.

With this issue, the object model becomes a real **Merkle DAG**: a commit's identity chains together the identities of its tree and its parents, so the entire history is tamper-evident and content-addressed. This is the piece that makes `git log` and `git checkout` possible (Phases 3-4).

## Conceptual background

In Git, a commit object's body is *text*, unlike the tree's binary-ish entries:

```
tree <hex sha256>
parent <hex sha256>
author <name> <email>

<message>
```

Details and design choices for bonsai:

- The **tree line is mandatory** and comes first: it is the snapshot this commit represents.
- A **parent line is repeated once per parent** and only appears if there is at least one parent. The initial commit has **no** parent lines.
- For simplicity bonsai **omits timestamps and timezone** (Git includes `author <...> <timestamp> <tz>`). This is a deliberate simplification: Git needs timestamps to disambiguate two commits of identical content made at different times; bonsai keeps determinism ("same content, same identity") as a teaching feature. If you want timestamps later, add an explicit `std::string timestamp` field — do **not** invent a default.
- The `<message>` is separated from the header block by **two newlines** (`\n\n`), exactly like Git. If the message is empty, the commit ends with `author ...\n\n` (that is, the trailing newline is still there).
- IDs are rendered as **lowercase hex** (use `Sha256::hex()`). Git stores the tree/parent lines as hex strings *within the commit text*; the commit itself is then hashed over those exact bytes.

### Why this is the DAG

A commit references parents **by their hashes**, never by embedding them. Following the parent chain from any commit walks the full history back to the initial commit. Because each commit's hash depends on its tree AND its parents' hashes, changing anything anywhere in history changes the hash of every descendant commit — that is what makes the graph tamper-evident. It is the same content-addressing principle you already used in `Tree`, now applied recursively across versions.

// Author of a commit: a plain value type (two strings).
struct Author {
    std::string name;
    std::string email;
};

class Commit : public Object {
public:
    Commit(bonsai::hash::Sha256 tree_id, Author author, std::string message);

    // Parents are added one at a time, in chronological order (oldest first).
    void add_parent(bonsai::hash::Sha256 parent_id);

    [[nodiscard]] std::string type() const override;                          // "commit"
    [[nodiscard]] std::vector<std::byte> serialize() const override;

    [[nodiscard]] const bonsai::hash::Sha256& tree_id() const noexcept;
    [[nodiscard]] std::span<const bonsai::hash::Sha256> parents() const noexcept;
    [[nodiscard]] const std::string& author_name() const noexcept;
    [[nodiscard]] const std::string& author_email() const noexcept;
    [[nodiscard]] const std::string& message() const noexcept;

private:
    bonsai::hash::Sha256 tree_id_;
    std::vector<bonsai::hash::Sha256> parents_;
    Author author_;
    std::string message_;
};

}  // namespace bonsai::objects
```

## Serialization format (canonical)

After the `"commit <len>\0"` header, the body is:

```
tree <hex tree id>\n
[parent <hex parent id>\n]   (repeated once per parent, only if any)
author <name> <email>\n
\n
<message>
```

Concretely, for a commit with tree id `T`, one parent `P`, author `A B <a@b>`, message `hi`:

```
tree T
parent P
author A B <a@b>

hi
```

The `\0` separating header from body is the same convention as Blob/Tree. The length in the header is the byte count of the body **excluding** the header itself.

Issue #1238: perf(semantic-search): evaluate TurboVec/TurboQuant as an optional vector index backend

## What problem does this solve?

As code graphs and cross-repository indexes grow, the semantic-search path could benefit from a lower-memory vector index without weakening retrieval quality or incremental indexing.

TurboVec implements Google Research's TurboQuant in Rust and advertises online ingestion, 2/4-bit compression, SIMD search, persistence, stable IDs, deletion, and allowlist filtering:

https://github.com/RyanCodrai/turbovec

The allowlist filtering is especially interesting for codebase-memory-mcp: structural/BM25/graph signals could narrow candidates, then dense retrieval could rerank only the allowed symbol IDs.

This is a recommendation to evaluate, not a request to replace the current implementation based on upstream benchmarks alone.

## Proposed solution

Create a bounded benchmark or design spike comparing the current semantic-search implementation against TurboVec/TurboQuant on representative code embeddings and repository sizes.

Measure:

- recall@k and ranking quality on code-symbol queries
- memory usage and persisted index size
- indexing and incremental-add latency
- deletion/update behavior
- single-query and batch-query latency
- filtered retrieval using graph-derived candidate IDs
- portability across Windows, Linux, macOS, x86, and ARM

Preserve these constraints:

- the pure-C, single-static-binary distribution remains the default
- AST, SQLite graph storage, BM25, and graph relationships remain unchanged
- no mandatory Rust runtime or external service
- no adoption unless project-owned benchmarks show a meaningful end-to-end gain

If results justify further work, possible paths include:

1. Port the relevant TurboQuant indexing/search algorithm to C.
2. Keep an optional experimental external backend behind a stable internal interface.
3. Adopt only the quantization or filtered-search ideas, not TurboVec itself.

## Alternatives considered

- Keep the current semantic-search implementation unchanged; this remains the correct baseline.
- FAISS adds a much larger native dependency and conflicts with the zero-dependency distribution goal.
- Integrating TurboVec directly would introduce Rust build and supply-chain complexity.
- Replacing SQLite or the graph model is unnecessary; this proposal concerns only dense vector retrieval.

Issue #1337: Allow circular references of project references

## Search Terms

circular reference project references graph

## Suggestion

Currently, project reference graphs are required to be acyclical because
 * Project references *imply* a `.d.ts` file is loaded, and `.d.ts` files can't exist before the build occurs
 * Only acyclic graphs can be topologically sorted

Both of these problems are solvable without too much work.

With the work done in #32028, we can effectively toggle the redirecting behavior, fixing the first issue. This would be done during the *initial* build phase only when an upstream project dependency isn't built yet.

The other problem is that project build order might not be predictable if we arbitrarily pick some starting point in the unsortable graph. This is fixable if we force solution authors to indicate which edges in the graph should be treated as ignored for the purposes of the topological sort:

```
    "references": [
        { "path": "../a" },
        { "path": "../b", "circular": true },
                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
        { "path": "../c" }
    ],
```

The benefits of this are:
 * In case of suboptimal `.d.ts` generation or memory pressure, developers can control where the "weak" link occurs in the build process
 * The build ordering is fully deterministic regardless of starting point
 * Graphs can't become "accidentally" circular - this is a clear opt-in

## Use Cases

`npm` and other package managers *do* allow circularities in dependency graphs, so this is apparently a thing.
We've also gotten feedback from some industry partners that they want to move to project references, but their dependency graph is circular in a way that would require a lot of work to "fix".

## Examples

Issue #29: cargo test --lib dies with SIGSEGV after output::tests::render_doctor_* stall (blocks v0.14.3)

## Summary

`cargo test` on the library target dies with **SIGSEGV**:

```
error: test failed, to rerun pass `--lib`

Caused by:
  process didn't exit successfully: `.../debug/build/eidetic-engine/<hash>/out/ee-<hash>`
  (signal: 11, SIGSEGV: invalid memory reference)
```

Most of the lib suite passes before the crash — `policy::store_auth`,
`policy::security_profile`, and `policy::swarm_slo_attribution` all report `ok`. The
process then dies rather than printing a `test result:` line, so there is no pass/fail
summary at all.

This blocks tagging `v0.14.3`: the build is clean and the binary is good, but the test
gate cannot be completed, and I am not willing to tag on a suite that segfaults.

## Environment

- Linux x86_64 build host, 128 cores
- commit `74ecd784c227e0f2add8a55f9b9493c080f43d3c`
- `cargo test` (full suite), `RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1`
- reproduced on two separate runs of the same commit

## Immediately before the crash

Two tests in the same module stall for over a minute right before the segfault:

```
test output::tests::render_doctor_concise_json_omits_diagnostic_firehose has been running for over 60 seconds
test output::tests::render_doctor_json_exposes_check_tier_and_advisory_summary has been running for over 60 seconds
```

Both are `output::tests::render_doctor_*`. Everything else in the visible tail completes
in milliseconds. A pair of tests hanging and then the harness dying is consistent with
those two being the trigger, though the harness runs tests in parallel so the crash is
not *proven* to be theirs.

## Why this is worth a careful look

The crate is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, so a segfault cannot come from unsafe code
written in `ee` itself. That leaves a short list:

1. **Stack exhaustion.** The most likely candidate. This crate has async chains deep
   enough that rustc's own trait resolution hit its recursion limit — the
   `recursion_depth_exceeding_limit` lint fires on
   `core::index::process_index_jobs_coalesced_with_cx_bounded` ->
   `process_index_jobs_with_drain` -> `process_one_index_job_with_cx` ->
   `process_one_index_job_after_snapshot_with_cx`, and I had to raise
   `recursion_limit` to 256 to get `clippy -D warnings` to pass. Async state machines
   that deep can also produce very large stack frames at runtime. Test threads get a
   smaller default stack (2 MiB) than the main thread, which is exactly why a crash
   like this shows up under the test harness and not in normal use.
2. **Unsafe code in a dependency** reached through these paths — the FrankenSQLite
   family or asupersync are the obvious candidates given what `render_doctor_*`
   exercises.
3. A genuine memory-safety bug in a dependency's FFI or allocator path.

I did **not** determine which. Everything above is a hypothesis; the only measured
facts are the SIGSEGV, the commit, and the two stalled tests.

## Suggested next steps

1. Run the two suspects alone and see whether either reproduces on its own:
   `cargo test --lib output::tests::render_doctor_concise_json_omits_diagnostic_firehose -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture`
2. If it reproduces, test the stack hypothesis cheaply by raising the harness stack:
   `RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 cargo test --lib`
   If a 32 MiB stack makes it pass, this is stack exhaustion, not memory corruption,
   and the fix is to box the large futures on those paths rather than to raise the
   stack permanently.
3. If it is not the stack, run the lib test binary under a debugger or ASan for a real
   backtrace. The binary path is printed in the failure message.
4. `--test-threads=1` is worth trying regardless — if the crash disappears, the
   interaction is between concurrently running tests rather than in one of them.

## Impact on releases

Blocks `v0.14.3`. Everything else for that release is verified good:

- version is `0.14.3` on `main`
- `cargo build` exits 0
- the resulting binary is `Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64` on macOS and reports
  `ee 0.14.3`
- the dependency-resolution failure that previously stopped the build outright is fixed

Only this segfault stands between the current tree and a tag.

Related: #28 (the full suite builds 552 binaries, which is why this takes hours to
surface).

Issue #879: Add recursive change reconstruction, review, and stacked-delivery workflow

## Goal

Add a Project Space / IDE workflow for **reconstructing a change set from zero trust**: every existing change starts outside the accepted result and must be explicitly looked at and re-added before it survives.

The workflow must work for:

- reviewing an already-implemented feature as if its code had never been read;
- recursively decomposing a large PR / branch into smaller reviewable pieces;
- splitting accepted work into multiple stacked PRs;
- pausing with large parts deliberately deferred and resuming later;
- periodically refactoring / reconstructing an entire codebase from a known-good checkpoint.

The core model is broader than PR review:

```text
Source / Candidate Change Set
          ↓
Recursive Decomposition Tree
          ↓
Explicit Reconstruction Review
          ↓
Reviewed Change Set / Tree
          ↓
Delivery Stack or New Codebase Checkpoint
```

Git branches, stashes, patches, and temporary commits are implementation details around this model.

## Zero-trust reconstruction rule

The key behavior is the opposite of a normal review.

Normal review implicitly trusts the candidate and looks for bad parts.

This workflow starts with **nothing implicitly accepted**:

```text
Candidate changes
      ↓
Unreviewed / Deferred pool
      ↓ explicit inspection
Accepted | Rejected | Deferred
```

A change only enters the reviewed result after the reviewer deliberately re-adds it.

This prevents an accidental earlier "approve all" state from bypassing the review. The workflow should make it impossible to claim complete reconstruction while unseen/deferred pieces remain.

## Recursive divide-and-conquer decomposition

A large change set can be split recursively until each piece is small enough to understand.

Example:

```text
Δ Feature
├── Backend
│   ├── Auth
│   │   ├── A1
│   │   └── A2
│   └── Persistence
│       ├── P1
│       └── P2
└── Frontend
    ├── F1
    └── F2
```

A split must be lossless. At every decomposition node:

```text
parent change set == composition of all child change sets
```

The complete leaf set must still reconstruct the original candidate:

```text
replay(all leaf pieces) == original feature/candidate tree
```

Splitting may be implemented with stashes, patches, temporary branches/commits, or another internal representation, but Project Space should expose the conceptual decomposition tree rather than force users to manage raw Git primitives manually.

Pieces may be decomposed by directory, file, hunk, symbol, semantic responsibility, dependency boundary, or another supported strategy.

## Review states

Every piece should have an explicit state:

- **Accepted** — deliberately reviewed and included in the reconstructed result;
- **Rejected** — deliberately reviewed and excluded;
- **Deferred** — intentionally not reviewed yet and available for later continuation.

The accounting invariant is:

```text
Accepted + Rejected + Deferred == original candidate change set
```

No piece may disappear silently.

Review completeness requires:

```text
Deferred == ∅
```

when the user wants to claim that the whole candidate has been reviewed.

A user may deliberately stop earlier and persist the reconstruction session with some parts deferred.

## Feature-branch review workflow

Given a feature branch, create a temporary local review workspace/branch from the known base/checkpoint.

Conceptually:

```bash
git switch <base>
git switch -c review/<feature>
git merge --squash <feature>
git reset --mixed
```

This places the complete feature change set into an unstaged working state.

The reviewer then explicitly reconstructs the desired result by accepting selected files/hunks/pieces and committing the reviewed tree.

The original feature branch remains unchanged during reconstruction.

The temporary review branch is local/disposable once the reviewed result and delivery output have been generated and verified.

## Final cleanup diff

After reconstruction:

```text
Original Feature Tree
        ↓
Reviewed Tree
```

The diff between them is the **cleanup diff**: everything that must be removed or changed on the original feature branch to make it equal the reviewed result.

This gives a strong post-condition:

```text
diff(feature, reviewed) == deliberately rejected/reworked cleanup
```

Applying that cleanup to the feature branch should produce the exact reviewed tree.

## Split accepted changes into stacked PRs

The reviewed change set can then be partitioned into multiple ordered delivery layers.

Example:

```text
base
 └─ pr-1        A
     └─ pr-2    A + B
         └─ pr-3 A + B + C

reviewed tree = A + B + C
```

For each new layer, derive the remaining candidate work from:

```text
diff(current stack head, reviewed tree)
```

The reviewer can select only the pieces that belong in that layer and defer the rest to later layers.

Final delivery completeness requires:

```text
tree(topmost stack branch) == tree(reviewed tree)
```

This proves that every accepted change was assigned somewhere in the stack.

The source-to-topmost diff should contain only deliberately rejected/reworked material.

## Codebase-wide refactoring / reconstruction

The same model must work against an entire codebase transformation, not only one PR.

Example:

```text
Known-good Checkpoint N
        ↓
large refactor / accumulated development
        ↓
Candidate Codebase
        ↓
recursive decomposition
        ↓
explicit reconstruction review
        ↓
Known-good Checkpoint N+1
```

The user may, for example, reconstruct only part of the backend first, leave the rest deferred, continue later, and recursively split remaining areas again.

This supports periodic "empty the box and deliberately put everything back" refactoring passes where every surviving change has been looked at again.

Git remains useful, but its long-term role changes.

Issue #96: diagnostics: XQST0054 circular variable dependency not detected

## Problem

16 QT4 test-cases (excluding the `fn:error()` artifact tracked in #87) across 2 files expect `XQST0054` ("a variable's initializing expression depends on itself") and we emit nothing.

## Root cause

Per the spec, it's a static error [err:XQST0054] if a module variable's initializing expression, directly or transitively (e.g. through a function call), depends on the variable's own value.

```xquery
declare namespace foo = "http://www.oracle.com/xquery/test";
declare variable $var1 as xs:integer := foo:price(xs:integer(2));
declare function foo:price ($b as xs:integer) as xs:integer { $var1 + 1 };
$var1
```
(`vardeclerr`) — `$var1`'s initializer calls `foo:price`, whose body references `$var1` — a cycle through a function call, not just a direct self-reference.

## Suggested fix

Build a dependency graph over module variables: for each `declare variable $v := expr`, find every module-variable reference reachable from `expr` (following into called user-declared function bodies, transitively) and flag `XQST0054` if `$v` is reachable from its own initializer. This needs a call graph, not just a syntactic walk, since the cycle here goes through a function body — worth checking whether `checkUndeclaredVariables`'s existing walker infrastructure can be reused/extended, or whether this needs a separate pass.

## Test cases

`vardeclerr` (`prod-VarDecl.snap`), `K2-InternalVariablesWithout-1`, plus the rest in `prod-VarDecl.snap`.

Issue #469: PERF-02 — Core operation benchmarks

## Context

The milestone asks that "Core operations have measured performance characteristics" and that "No critical operation exhibits unacceptable behavior at the intended MVP scale." The value is in having numbers at all: without them, "is this slow?" is answered by opinion, and a regression is only noticed when someone complains.

Some coverage exists — `hot_paths_perf_test.go` and `reach_out_trigger_perf_test.go` — but as scattered tests rather than a suite with recorded baselines.

The operations worth measuring are the ones whose cost grows with data, not the ones that happen to be called often:

- contact list with pagination, filters, and sorting
- contact detail, which assembles the full nested `Card` plus projections
- FTS search across `contacts_fts`, `notes_fts`, `activities_fts`
- relationship traversal, especially multi-hop and through dense hubs
- the dashboard and its aggregates
- reach-out and cadence computation over the whole contact set
- duplicate detection, which is inherently pairwise and the most likely quadratic surprise
- contact merge, which repoints every association
- delete cascade, which enumerates every dependent table by hand

## Recommended actions

1. Benchmark each operation at each profile from #468, recording wall-clock time and query count. Query count matters as much as duration: an N+1 that is invisible at 100 contacts is the thing that breaks at 10,000, and it shows up in the count long before it shows up in the clock.
2. Run against a real migrated schema (CLAUDE.md trap #1). Index behavior is the entire subject here, and `AutoMigrate` does not reproduce the hand-written indexes or the FTS triggers.
3. Record baselines as committed data so change is visible over time, rather than printing numbers into a CI log nobody reads. #471 turns these into budgets; this ticket produces the measurements.
4. Look for the shape of the cost, not just its value. Measure each operation at two or more scales and check whether it grows linearly — a quadratic operation that is fast at the typical profile is a future outage, and it is only detectable by comparing across scales.
5. Measure the pathological records specifically, not just the average. The contact with forty phones and a hundred relationships is a real user's real contact.
6. Include the write path, not only reads: create, update, and merge under the concurrency `loadsmoke` already exercises, since write contention on SQLite is a different constraint from read cost.

## How to verify

- Every listed operation has a recorded measurement at every profile.
- Query counts are recorded alongside durations.
- Growth across scales is recorded, and any super-linear operation is flagged as a finding, not just a number.
- Benchmarks run against the real migrated schema.
- Baselines are committed and diffable.
- Hand-verify per CLAUDE.md: introduce an N+1 into one endpoint and confirm the query-count assertion catches it. Restore.

Issue #330: Recursive CTE support: WithRecursive API, WITH RECURSIVE dialect gating, CTE self-reference binding

## Summary

Recursive CTEs are not supported and are **not expressible** through the current API. There is no `RECURSIVE` token anywhere in the codebase — not in the generator, the runtime, the shared SQL parser, or the dialect config. This is an absence rather than a defect: users have no way to write one, so nothing silently mis-compiles today.

This issue tracks implementing the full `WithRecursive` feature as designed below.

## Current state

Non-recursive CTEs are largely complete, and a meaningful amount of the required machinery already exists:

| Existing capability | Location |
|---|---|
| `CteDef` / `CteColumn` IR (inner SQL, DTO-derived columns, carrier parameter offset) | `src/Quarry.Generator/IR/CteDef.cs` |
| `WITH "x" AS (…)` rendering (three call sites) | `src/Quarry.Generator/IR/SqlAssembler.cs:216`, `:426`, `:1614` |
| Inner-plan re-render with rebased parameter offset (multi-CTE `@p0` collision fix) | `SqlAssembler.cs:243-256` |
| CTE definition/resolution, QRY080/081/082 | `src/Quarry.Generator/Parsing/ChainAnalyzer.cs:754-987` |
| DTO column resolution | `src/Quarry.Generator/IR/CteDtoResolver.cs`, called from `UsageSiteDiscovery.cs:3883-3885` |
| Runtime stubs (`With<TDto>`, `With<TEntity,TDto>`, `FromCte<TDto>`) | `src/Quarry/Context/QuarryContext.cs:150`, `:164`, `:174`; `QuarryContext<TSelf>` overrides at `:644`, `:652` |
| CTE→CTE joins (`FromCte<A>().Join<B>(…)`) | existing, covered by tests |
| Set operations render inline inside a CTE body | `SqlAssembler.cs:287-299` |

That last row matters: `UNION ALL` inside a CTE body is essentially free — the operand rendering path is already recursive over `QueryPlan`.

## Blockers

### 1. No way to self-reference the CTE (the dominant cost)

The recursive member needs `FROM cte JOIN base ON …`. Two things prevent it:

- The `With` lambda is `Func<IEntityAccessor<TDto>, IQueryBuilder<TDto>>` — there is no handle on the CTE currently being defined.
- `FromCte<TDto>()` resolution iterates **forward** and requires a matching `CteDef` to already exist in the list, otherwise it emits QRY081 (`ChainAnalyzer.cs:962-986`). A self-reference violates that ordering by construction.

Work required: a new entry point, a new `InterceptorKind`, discovery wiring in `UsageSiteDiscovery` (the `With`/`FromCte` dispatch is name-based at `UsageSiteDiscovery.cs:3871`), and a binder path where the chain root is a CTE rather than a schema entity. `CallSiteBinder.cs:126-134` already carries a "DTO is not a schema entity" fallback for CTE chains — that is the hook — but column binding against `CteDef.Columns` instead of `EntityInfo` is new code.

### 2. `WITH RECURSIVE` keyword + dialect gating

`"WITH "` is a hardcoded string literal at all three `SqlAssembler` sites listed above. PostgreSQL, SQLite, and MySQL 8+ require `WITH RECURSIVE`; SQL Server forbids the keyword entirely. The keyword is per-`WITH`-clause, not per-CTE, so the flag belongs on the plan (or is derived as "any `CteDef.IsRecursive`"), plus a capability on `SqlDialectConfig` (`src/Quarry.Generator/Sql/SqlDialectConfig.cs`). MySQL 8.0 minimum is not knowable at compile time — document it.

Small: roughly 50 LOC plus the config field.

### 3. CTE bodies emit no column aliases

Current output (`src/Quarry.Tests/SqlOutput/CrossDialectCteTests.cs:40`):

```sql
WITH "Order" AS (SELECT "OrderId", "UserId", "Total", … FROM "orders" WHERE "Total" > 100)
SELECT "OrderId", "Total" FROM "Order"
```

This works only because DTO property names happen to coincide with column names. Recursive members compute values (`n.Depth + 1`, path concatenation) that have no natural column name, and the anchor and recursive members must produce identically-named columns.

Recommended fix: emit an explicit column list — `WITH RECURSIVE "cte"("A","B") AS (…)`. One loop over `CteDef.Columns`, valid on all four dialects, and simpler than retrofitting `AS` alias emission into the projection renderer.

### 4. Recursion-specific semantics

- SQL Server defaults to `MAXRECURSION 100` and hard-errors past it. The escape hatch is `OPTION (MAXRECURSION n)`, which **must be the final clause** of the outer statement — this interacts with pagination and `Prepare()` render ordering.
- Validation the engines require anyway, surfaced as compile-time diagnostics instead of runtime errors: recursive member references the CTE exactly once; no aggregates / `DISTINCT` / `ORDER BY` / `LIMIT` in the recursive member; no outer join to the CTE; anchor member may not reference the CTE.

## Proposed API

```csharp
public class EmployeeSchema : Schema
{
    public static string Table => "employees";
    public Key<int> EmployeeId => Identity();
    public Col<string> Name => Length(100);
    public Ref<EmployeeSchema, int?> ManagerId => ForeignKey<EmployeeSchema, int?>();
}

public record EmployeeNode(int EmployeeId, string Name, int Depth);
```

```csharp
var tree = await db
    .WithRecursive<Employee, EmployeeNode>(
        anchor:  e    => e.Where(x => x.ManagerId.Id == null)
                          .Select(x => new EmployeeNode(x.EmployeeId, x.Name, 0)),
        recurse: node => node.Join<Employee>((n, e) => n.EmployeeId == e.ManagerId.Id)
                             .Select((n, e) => new EmployeeNode(e.EmployeeId, e.Name, n.Depth + 1)))
    .FromCte<EmployeeNode>()
    .Where(n => n.Depth < maxDepth)
    .OrderBy(n => n.Depth).ThenBy(n => n.Name)
    .ExecuteFetchAllAsync();
```

The `recurse` lambda has the **same signature shape** as today's `With<TDto>` — `Func<IEntityAccessor<TDto>, IQueryBuilder<TDto>>` — the accessor is simply bound to the CTE instead of a table. Everything after `.FromCte<T>()` is the existing chain API.

Useful type-system property: SQL requires the anchor and recursive members to be union-compatible and normally reports the mismatch at runtime. Here both lambdas are constrained to return `IQueryBuilder<…, EmployeeNode>`, so C# rejects a mismatch before the generator runs.

Issue #147: Recompile only what changed: a reverse dependency walk, structural sharing, and a differential test

## Summary

Add `compile_incremental`: given the previous snapshot and a `ChangeSet`, mark the affected units dirty by
walking the fixed four-level dependency graph, rebuild only those, and share every unchanged subtree by
`Arc` clone. Prove it correct with a differential property test asserting the incremental result is
semantically identical to a full compile of the same bundle, and gate it with the two numbers that matter:
a one-route change against a live 100,000-route table, and the allocation count of everything except the
route table.

## Context

Incremental compile is architectural, not an optimisation. It is what dictates that `Snapshot` is a tree of
`Arc`s and that resources carry content hashes, so retrofitting it means rewriting the snapshot type. It is
also the single most defensible differentiator in this milestone: Kong shipped full-configuration broadcast
for years, found it to be the binding constraint on propagation delay, memory and CPU, then fixed it in
Gateway 3.10 and, per Kong's own documentation, made incremental configuration sync available only in
Kong Enterprise and not supported in Kong OSS. Traefik still recomputes the entire merged configuration per
provider event with a full structural compare and several deep copies. Shipping incremental sync in the open
source core is a direct, defensible advantage, and this issue is where it becomes true.

The dependency graph is fixed, shallow and known at compile time:

```
Certificate  -> Listener            (through the certificate references)
Upstream     -> ClusterSnapshot     (endpoints and transport)
Listener     -> Route               (hostname intersection and attachment)
Route        -> RouteTable          (the compiled table)
Role         -> nothing in the data plane
```

Three properties of that graph do the work:

1. **An endpoint change dirties no route.** `ClusterId` is keyed on the upstream's resource identity, so
   changing an upstream's endpoints, weights or health rebuilds one `ClusterSnapshot` and leaves every route
   that references it byte-identical. This is what makes an EndpointSlice storm cost O(changed endpoints)
   rather than O(routes). It is also the answer to the fan-out worry: an upstream referenced by every route
   is marked dirty once, at the upstream, and never propagated to the routes.
2. **A role change compiles nothing.** RBAC is evaluated by the admin API, not by the data plane, so a role
   edit publishes a snapshot in which every field is `Arc::ptr_eq` with the previous one. The publish still
   happens, because the bundle version must advance and the audit trail must record it.
3. **A certificate change touches listeners, never routes.** The TLS material is rebuilt and the route table
   is shared verbatim.

For the route table itself, the router already provides the incremental machinery:
`RouteTableBuilder::rebuild_from(previous, generation)` reuses by `Arc` clone every group whose content hash,
chain successor, name set and pattern list are unchanged, and it is documented to produce a table
byte-identical to a full build. Our job is to feed it and to decide when it is safe to call, not to
re-implement group reuse.

One honest limitation, stated here so nobody chases a number that is not available: `add_http_route` takes a
route by value, so an incremental compile still re-admits every route, which is an O(n) pass with a small
constant. The trie building, the group arenas and the literal blobs are what `rebuild_from` avoids, and they
are the expensive part. Making admission itself incremental requires a router-side API that accepts a
previously admitted route set, which is a router change and is out of scope here. The benchmark therefore
reports the re-admission cost separately rather than hiding it inside a headline number.

## Problem

The CLI and the web app use different rules to discover skills.

The CLI scans skill directories recursively and follows directory symlinks. The web skill library checks only this path:

```text
<skill-root>/<direct-child>/SKILL.md
```

This difference prevents the web app and rooms from finding skills inside a repository-level symlink.

## Example

```text
~/.agents/skills/agent-skills -> ~/Projekte/agent-skills
~/Projekte/agent-skills/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md
```

With this structure:

- The CLI finds 72 skills.
- The web API finds 24 direct skills.
- The web app misses 48 skills below the `agent-skills` symlink.

A symlink that points directly to one skill works. A symlink that points to a repository or collection does not work.

## Expected behavior

The CLI, web skill library, and rooms should use the same recursive discovery rules. This behavior also matches Pi, Claude Code, and Codex.

## Current implementation

The CLI loader recursively calls `loadSkillsFromDirInternal()` and resolves symlinks with `realPath()`:

```text
runtime/packages/agent/src/harness/skills.ts
```

The web library reads only direct children and checks `path.join(dir, entry.name, "SKILL.md")`:

```text
apps/web-server/src/index.ts
```

The current symlink test covers only a direct symlink to one skill. It does not cover a symlink to a directory that contains several skills:

```text
apps/web-server/scripts/skills-shared-dir-smoke.ts
```

I reproduced the API result locally with v0.8.0. The same non-recursive web discovery code is present in v0.10.1 (`2963a17d9d4b58581d94a8b954511a5c04bb870a`).

## Suggested change

Use the recursive runtime discovery rules for the web skill library and room skill resolution.

Please keep these existing rules:

- Skip dot directories and `node_modules`.
- Honor ignore files.
- Keep the current source precedence.
- Prevent loops when symlinks point back to a parent directory.
- Use the same resolved manifest path for listing, enabling, and fingerprint checks.

## Acceptance criteria

- The web library finds skills in nested directories.
- The web library follows a symlink to a repository or skill collection.
- Direct skill symlinks continue to work.
- The CLI and web app list the same skills for the same configured roots.
- A symlink loop does not hang the scan.

Pi users lose durable, directory-specific knowledge between sessions. A maintainer on the project Evokoa/pgGraph (Rust) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #23: shortest_path() has no edge_types filter, unlike expand()/traverse()

## Summary

`graph.shortest_path()` and `graph.weighted_shortest_path()` take no `edge_types` argument, while `graph.expand()` and `graph.traverse()` do. There is no way to restrict a shortest path to a subset of relationship types.

```sql
graph.shortest_path(
  source_table regclass,
  source_id text,
  target_table regclass,
  target_id text,
  max_depth int DEFAULT 20,
  hydrate boolean DEFAULT true
)
```

## Why it matters

Relationship-typed shortest path is the common shape of the query. "How is this chunk connected to that chunk *through shared entities*" is a different question from "how is it connected through any edge", and only the first is usually meaningful.

The current workaround is to register and build a second property graph containing only the wanted edge types, then `select_graph()` before querying. That works, but:

- On a 1.29M node / 3.2M edge graph the restricted build took **~55 s** (`build_graph()` → `nodes_loaded=1288553 edges_loaded=3199812 build_time_ms=54611`).
- It produces a second on-disk artifact and a second in-memory projection, so the cost is per relationship-type combination rather than per query.
- With `max_loaded_graphs_per_backend = 1`, alternating between the full graph and the restricted graph inside one backend causes unload/reload, so callers need connection pinning to avoid it.

## How I hit it

I was comparing `shortest_path()` against a hand-written recursive CTE on the same tables. My graph had two edge types (`m_chunk`/`m_entity` from a junction table, plus `has_chunk`). Without edge-type restriction the two engines were answering different questions — `shortest_path()` was routing through `has_chunk`, producing shorter paths than the MENTIONS-only CTE. Path lengths disagreed on 6 of 6 sampled pairs until I rebuilt a MENTIONS-only graph, after which they matched exactly on all 6.

That is a correctness trap for anyone benchmarking or cross-checking `shortest_path()` against another engine, since nothing in the signature signals that all edge types participate.

## Request

Add `edge_types text[] DEFAULT NULL` to `shortest_path()` and `weighted_shortest_path()`, with the same semantics as in `expand()`/`traverse()` (NULL = all types). This would also remove the need for per-type graph registration in the common case.

If restricting inside the CSR traversal is not straightforward, even documenting the current behavior in `api-reference.mdx` — "all registered edge types participate; register a separate graph to restrict" — would prevent the mismatch above.

## Environment

`ghcr.io/evokoa/pggraph:1.0.0`, PostgreSQL 17.10, linux/arm64.

A maintainer on the project FabianPlum/SMILify (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #95: Weld step in apply_modifiers can silently destroy large parts of sparse / fragmented meshes

## Title
Weld modifier in `apply_modifiers` silently destroys mesh geometry on sparse/patchy scans

## Summary
**Quick fix available:** item 4 below is a trivial one-line bug (hardcoded threshold). Items 1–3 are a small design change to make Weld connectivity-aware. A branch with fixes for all four is linked at the bottom.

## Problem
In `apply_modifiers()` (in `custom_processing/prepare_antscan_data_for_mesh_fitting.py`), an Edge Split modifier is followed by a Weld modifier. On some ant scans, the Weld step merges vertices across regions that should stay separate, destroying large parts of the mesh. This happens silently ; no error is raised, and processing continues with a corrupted result.

## Root causes

1. **Weld threshold is based only on bounding-box size.**
   The threshold is computed as `0.2%` of the largest dimension of the object. This assumes a solid, densely and uniformly triangulated mesh. After the preceding ray-cast cleaning step, the mesh is often sparse or patchy; for the same overall size, the "safe" merge distance is then much smaller. Using the bbox-only value causes Weld to bridge gaps between surfaces that should remain disconnected.

2. **Small debris islands are still present when Weld runs.**
   Ray-cast cleaning can leave tiny disconnected fragments. Weld has no knowledge of connectivity and merges them into real geometry, creating degenerate topology.

3. **No safety check on face loss.**
   If Weld collapses a large fraction of the faces (a clear sign it merged across disconnected regions), the pipeline doesn't detect it and continues silently.

4. **Bug: explicit threshold is ignored.**
   When a caller passes an explicit `weld_merge_threshold`, the value is discarded and hard-coded to `2`.

## Observed impact
On certain AntScan models, the processed mesh loses substantial real geometry (thin necks, legs, antennae bases, etc.) with no warning in the logs. Downstream fitting steps then operate on a broken surface.

## Direction of a fix
- [ ] Derive the Weld threshold from both bounding-box size and local mesh density (median edge length); use the more conservative of the two
- [ ] Remove small connected components before Weld runs, so debris can't be fused into real geometry
- [ ] Abort with a clear error if Weld destroys more than a configurable percentage of faces
- [ ] Fix the hardcoded `weld_merge_threshold = 2` to respect the caller-supplied value
- [ ] *(Optional, related hardening of the ray-cast stage)* Expand the neighbourhood kept around each ray hit, and reconnect genuine thin anatomical connections via paths that already exist in the original mesh

A branch exploring these changes is available here:
https://github.com/khaoulaJel/SMILify/tree/fix/apply-modifiers-weld

Normal DIMS path:

**RAD → RAC → DEA → Execute → Execution Performance Metrics → Verified Outcome**

Actual physical hazard path only:

**RAD → RAC → APN (using CEI) → Abatement Priority**

### RAD™ — Risk Assessment Dome
RAD is the DIMS cross-system risk-assessment service/workspace. It supports governed assessment of physical and non-physical risk using Severity × Probability and produces a RAC.

### RAC — Risk Assessment Code
RAC expresses the assessed risk category. Lower RAC numbers normally receive higher primary risk priority.

### DEA™ — DIMS Execution Algorithm
DEA determines relative execution order after RAC and required governance/readiness gates. When executable items share the same RAC, DEA should discriminate from objective system-recorded facts such as verified blocking dependencies, recorded deadlines, waiting age, readiness, continuity, and other validated system-derived signals.

The former **EPI — Execution Priority Index is retired as a separate active layer**. DEA owns execution ordering. Do not reintroduce subjective user-entered EPI ratings.

### Execution Performance Metrics
Execution Performance Metrics measure how work was actually executed and remain separate from DEA. Active measures include HEI, AEL, RWL, VOY, Autonomy, and Session Window. They are observed during/after execution; they do not determine RAC and do not replace DEA execution ordering.
