# `cover` vs. the CoRIM Reference Verification Algorithm

A conformance comparison between the **`cover`** (COrim VERifier) proof‑of‑concept
implementation and the **reference verifier algorithm** defined by the CoRIM
Internet‑Draft.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Implementation** | [`repos/cover`](../repos/cover) — `cover` v0.0.1, Rust (edition 2024) |
| **Impl. commit** | `030bc2db23bbc58e72c4764ea004e98a19199705` (2026‑04‑29) |
| **Spec** | [`repos/extra/draft-ietf-rats-corim-11.txt`](../repos/extra/draft-ietf-rats-corim-11.txt) — `draft-ietf-rats-corim-11`, "Concise Reference Integrity Manifest" (July 2026) |
| **Relevant spec sections** | §8.1 (Logical Phases), §8.2 (The CoRIM Processor) |
| **Report date** | 2026‑07‑20 |
| **Impl. size** | ~2,938 LOC across `src/lib/*.rs` |

> **Read this first — version drift.** `cover`'s own README states it follows
> *"CoRIM draft spec (rev 8.) Section 9"*. The document compared here is
> **rev 11**, where the algorithm moved to **§8.2** and the data structures and
> relation set were reworked. Some divergences below are simply the implementation
> tracking an older draft, not defects. The spec text itself is still marked in
> places with `[TBC]`/`[TODO]` editor notes, so exact conformance is a moving target.

---

## 1. Executive summary

`cover` is a faithful but **partial** realisation of the reference algorithm. It
implements the ECT‑centric internal model and the core of **Phases 2–4** (Evidence
augmentation, Reference‑Value corroboration, Endorsed‑Value augmentation) for a
single attestation scheme (Arm CCA), then hands the resulting **ACS** to a Rego
policy engine to synthesise an **EAR/AR4SI** attestation result in lieu of the
spec's out‑of‑scope "subsequent phases".

**What matches well**
- ECT (Environment‑Claim Tuple) as the central internal construct, with
  `cm-type` mirroring the spec's `cmtype` (evidence / reference-values / endorsements).
- Triple → relation transformation (`rv`, `ev`, `evs`) mirrors §8.2.3.7.
- ACS initialised from Evidence, then RV corroboration copying the matched
  ACS element‑list into the addition ECT — matches §8.2.4.2.1.
- Additions carry the CoRIM signer as **authority** (RVP / Endorser authority).
- Conditional Endorsement **Series** uses first‑match‑wins semantics (§8.2.4.3.2).

**Most significant divergences / gaps**
1. **No staging‑area ordering / topological sort / fixpoint** (§8.2.4.1) — single fixed pass.
2. **`ev` condition matching logic is stricter than the spec** and looks buggy (see §5.1).
3. **Authority is deliberately *not* used as matching criteria** (§8.2.4.4) — `authorized-by` conditions are ignored.
4. **No `keys`, `dm`, or `td` relations** — identity keys, domain‑membership and trust‑dependency triples are unimplemented; attest keys are shoe‑horned into a private ECT extension.
5. **No `CHECK`/consistency step and no atomic append** (§8.2.4, Figure 48).
6. **Phase 1 is minimal**: no validity‑window checks, no CoTL/CoTS, no profile‑based CoRIM selection; only **signed** CoRIMs; only the **CCA** scheme.

---

## 2. Scope and method

The comparison covers the algorithm proper — the "CoRIM Processor" of §8.2 —
which the spec frames as producing the ACS and handing it off (§8.2.5). Subsequent
phases (consistency checks, Appraisal Policy for Evidence, result emission) are
explicitly **out of scope** of the spec algorithm, so `cover`'s Rego/EAR pipeline is
assessed only for consistency of intent, not line‑by‑line conformance.

A maintainer on the project wwestlake/Creation-Suite (C++) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #59: Epic: CEL modules - module_decl, namespacing, save/reuse/reference as assets

See shared/CEL/docs/CEL_V2_LANGUAGE_SPEC.md section 6 (and section 5.1 for the module_decl grammar) for the full spec — this issue tracks implementation, the doc is the source of truth for design intent.

## Goal
Modules that can be saved, reused, and referenced across projects and apps — without turning CEL into a separate-compilation language. CEL stays single-compilation-unit (the whole point of the language is a sub-second full rebuild); "modularity" here means source organization and cross-project/cross-app reuse, not a build/link system.

## Grammar: module_decl
```
module_decl:
    "module" IDENT IDENT "{" decl_list "}"
```
Module name, then a domain/type tag (`general`, `audio-dsp`, `sequencer`, ...  — see #56's per-module domain checking), wrapping the existing decl_list. One file is one module block. The module's name IS its namespace for qualified references (`vecutils::foo`) — no separate namespace keyword.

## Import forms
- Local: `import "vec_utils.cel" as vecutils;` — same project, simple path.
- Asset-referenced: `import module("<asset-id>") as vecutils;` — resolved through shared/AssetSystem's existing catalog/resolver and, for cross-app cases, shared/Interop's ProjectRegistry (the same discovery mechanism relevant to Suite #13/Movie #16/#17, currently unconsumed by any app). A CEL module becomes a new AssetKind (alongside foleyPatch etc.) rather than a bespoke resolution system.

## Design decisions
- Namespacing is qualified (`vecutils::foo`), not flat — avoids collisions once independently-authored shared modules accumulate. Purely compile-time (name resolution within the single compiled program), zero runtime cost.
- A "module asset" is reusable, addressable source (or a cached AST) — not a separately linked binary.
- Visibility: leaning toward explicit-export-only over C-style visible-by-default, for the same collision-avoidance reason as qualified namespacing — not yet finalized.
- Cross-file `rec` mutual-recursion cycle detection (#57) needs no special handling — the call graph doesn't care which file a function's text lives in, since it's still one compiled unit.
- Asset-catalog metadata for a celModule asset (including its domain tag) is derived from the in-source module_decl at save time, not authored separately — source is primary, the asset record mirrors it.

## Explicitly deferred, not decided
Versioning: what happens when a shared module a project depends on changes underneath it? Simplest v1 answer is "always resolves to the asset's current state, no versioning" — acceptable to start, not final.

## Sequencing
Depends on #49 (math types) existing to be worth reusing as a first real shared module, and benefits from — but doesn't strictly require — Suite #13 (ProjectRegistry finally being consumed by an app) for the cross-app import form specifically; local/same-project imports don't need that gap closed first.

Issue #10: feat: add task DAG representation and dependency-aware compile planning

## Motivation

`task_tree` intentionally models a simple hierarchy where every non-root task has exactly one direct parent. This keeps construction, failure propagation, and slot lifetimes easy to reason about, but it cannot express workflows where one task depends on multiple upstream results.

The repository already lists DAG support as future work. This issue tracks the next structural step: add a DAG representation while preserving YOrch's core model of **describe dependencies -> `compile_plan(...)` -> execute a precomputed plan**.

## Goals

- Introduce a task-graph/DAG representation that can express multiple direct predecessors.
- Preserve `task_tree` as the simple tree-oriented API rather than forcing every tree user into a general graph builder.
- Compile graph structure into an execution plan with dependency/readiness information prepared ahead of execution.
- Validate graph invariants before execution, including cycle detection and invalid dependency references.
- Define argument-source semantics when a task consumes values from more than one predecessor.
- Keep graph metadata statically analyzable where possible so execution does not become a fully dynamic scheduler by default.

## Design questions

- Should the public type be `task_graph`, or should graph support be expressed through a more general task-structure abstraction?
- How should nodes receive stable identities for declaring edges without making the builder cumbersome?
- How should `borrow_prev`, `copy_prev`, `consume_prev`, and related APIs generalize when there are multiple predecessors?
- How should fanout and slot lifetime analysis work across joins?
- Should cycle rejection happen entirely at compile time for statically built graphs, during `compile_plan(...)`, or both depending on construction mode?
- How should failure propagate through joins when only a subset of predecessors succeed?

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A minimal diamond dependency can be represented: `A -> {B, C} -> D`.
- [ ] `D` cannot execute until all declared predecessors required by the plan have completed successfully.
- [ ] Cycles and invalid dependency references are rejected before execution.
- [ ] Existing `task_tree` APIs and behavior remain source-compatible.
- [ ] Graph compilation produces explicit dependency/readiness metadata used by the executor.
- [ ] Tests cover chains, fanout, joins, invalid graphs, failure propagation, and mixed payload types.
- [ ] Documentation explains when to use `task_tree` vs DAG/task graph.
- [ ] Add at least a small benchmark baseline for DAG plan compilation/execution overhead.

## Non-goals

Async or parallel scheduling is not required to complete this issue. A DAG should first have well-defined structure and serial execution semantics; async/parallel execution can build on the same compiled dependency model in separate work.

Issue #2: lib: add process-rooted closure analysis for inherited DT_RPATH

# lib: add process-rooted closure analysis for inherited DT_RPATH

## Problem

The current analyzer treats every package-owned ELF object as an independent consumer.

For each object, it compiles a resolver plan from:

* that object’s own `DT_RPATH` or `DT_RUNPATH`;
* explicit process search directories;
* configured and default directories;
* package-local extension directories.

This is appropriate for package-wide edge auditing, but it cannot model one important part of runtime-loader behavior:

* `DT_RUNPATH` applies only to the direct dependencies of the object carrying it;
* `DT_RPATH`, when not superseded by `DT_RUNPATH`, may remain available while resolving descendants in the dependency closure.

Correct resolution may therefore depend on the executable or shared object from which loading began.

The same shared object can resolve a dependency differently under two different process roots. A report keyed only by consumer object and `DT_NEEDED` name cannot represent that distinction.

## Target

Add a separate process-rooted closure-analysis interface that traverses dependency graphs from explicit entry objects and carries inherited loader context through the traversal.

The existing package-wide `analyzer::run()` interface should remain available with its current edge-local meaning.

## Proposed direction

Introduce a distinct analysis operation rather than silently changing the semantics of existing reports.

A possible public shape is:

```cpp
struct closure_request {
  std::vector<object_path> entry_objects;
  target_profile target;
};

closure_report closure_analyzer::run(
    const inventory& consumers,
    const provider_ownership& ownership,
    const resolver_config& resolver,
    elf_backend& backend,
    closure_request request) const;
```

Each traversal node needs enough context to distinguish:

* the entry object that began the closure;
* the current consumer object;
* inherited `DT_RPATH` directories;
* the resolved provider path;
* the dependency name;
* observation failures encountered under that closure.

The resolver context should evolve as follows:

* an object with `DT_RUNPATH` uses it for its direct dependencies but does not pass it to children;
* an object with `DT_RPATH` and no `DT_RUNPATH` contributes its expanded RPATH to descendant resolution;
* explicit process, configured, cache, default, and package-local inputs remain caller-controlled;
* `DF_1_NODEFLIB`, target profiles, hwcaps ordering, and provider compatibility continue to apply normally.

## Invariants

* Results depend only on explicit caller-supplied facts.
* The library does not inspect the running process environment.
* The library does not execute the entry object.
* Traversal order does not affect report ordering.
* Dependency cycles terminate deterministically.
* Repeated objects may be revisited when their inherited resolver context differs.
* Candidate observations remain reusable within one analysis run.
* Provider ownership remains independent of consumer selection.
* Incomplete observations remain distinct from unresolved dependencies.

## Report identity

A closure finding must not collapse two edges merely because they share:

```text
consumer object + DT_NEEDED name
```

The finding identity must also retain the process root or equivalent resolver context when that context can change the selected provider.

For example:

```text
/app/a -> /usr/lib/libchild.so -> libprivate.so
/app/b -> /usr/lib/libchild.so -> libprivate.so
```

may legitimately select different providers when `/app/a` and `/app/b` establish different inherited RPATH state.

## Non-goals

* Do not replace the existing package-wide linkage analyzer.
* Do not model `dlopen()`, `dlmopen()`, or arbitrary runtime namespaces initially.
* Do not model symbol lookup, interposition, relocation, constructors, or ABI versioning in this issue.
* Do not infer entry objects from package metadata.
* Do not read ambient `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.
* Do not add package-manager transaction policy to the library.

## Acceptance criteria

* An entry executable’s `DT_RPATH` can resolve a grandchild dependency.
* The same executable’s `DT_RUNPATH` cannot resolve that grandchild unless the intermediate object supplies its own applicable path.
* `DT_RUNPATH` suppresses the same object’s `DT_RPATH`.
* Two entry objects can produce different provider resolutions for the same child object and needed name.
* Cyclic dependency graphs terminate and produce deterministic reports.
* Shared subgraphs are reused when their resolver context is equivalent.
* Different inherited contexts are not incorrectly merged.
* Missing and malformed observations preserve report incompleteness.
* Existing `analyzer::run()` behavior and tests remain unchanged.
* The new semantics are documented in `libpkgimpact(3)` and `pkgimpact(7)`.
